title: A critical appraisal of clinical practice guidelines on insomnia using the RIGHT statement and AGREE II instrument.
authors: Zhu H, Li M, Pan B et al.
conditions: chronic insomnia (adults, children, ASD, ICU, cancer, pregnancy/menopause)
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 26 insomnia CPGs worldwide (searched PubMed, WoS, Embase, 3 Chinese databases, 6 guideline-developer databases); countries not listed in abstract
keyFindings: 26 CPGs; 22 used nine different grading systems; 53.85% rated 'recommended with modification', 2 'recommended'; clarity of presentation highest domain (67.9% ± 11.04%), applicability lowest (37.1% ± 12.67%); mean RIGHT reporting rate 67.87%.
conflictsOfInterest: Abstract: no COI statement in PubMed record; Lanzhou University / WHO Collaborating Centre authors.
notes: Quality appraisal only; does not compare what guidelines recommend about drugs. Paywalled; table of included guidelines and countries needs full text.

title: Systematic Review of Clinical Practice Guidelines for Insomnia Disorder.
authors: Seow SY, Kwok KFV, Tay KH et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 10 insomnia CPG records (PubMed, EMBASE, guideline repositories, society websites); exact guidelines/countries not listed in abstract
keyFindings: 10 records; 4 CPGs high and 3 moderate overall quality (AGREE II + AGREE-REX); most recommend drugs only if CBT-I unavailable, unsuccessful or declined; 'Recommendations on types of medicines and dose and duration of treatment varied and were nonspecific'; 'The CPGs diverged in the choice of first-line pharmacotherapy'.
conflictsOfInterest: Authors declare no conflicts of interest.
notes: Closest existing item to a drug-level guideline comparison, built as a 'recommendation matrix'. Singapore authors. Small set; paywalled; pre-dates 2023 European update, 2024 Canadian Delphi, 2025 deprescribing guidelines and orexin-antagonist approvals in many countries.

title: Efficacy and safety of pharmacotherapy in chronic insomnia: A review of clinical guidelines and case reports.
authors: Del Rio Verduzco A, Salari A, Haghparast P
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 3 clinical guidelines (US-focused; abstract does not name them) plus 15 case reports and 13 clinical studies
keyFindings: All 3 guidelines rated most drug recommendations weak except CBT-I; 15 case reports and 13 clinical studies reviewed for safety.
conflictsOfInterest: Authors declare no potential conflict of interest.
notes: Pharmacist-oriented, US lens; not a country comparison.

title: A systematic review and quality assessment of complementary and alternative medicine recommendations in insomnia clinical practice guidelines.
authors: Ng JY, Parakh ND
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: Adult insomnia CPGs 2009-2020 (MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, GIN, NCCIH, NICE, ECRI)
keyFindings: 277 results, 250 unique; 9 CPGs mentioned CAM, 6 made CAM recommendations; AGREE II domains ranked scope & purpose > clarity > editorial independence > stakeholder involvement > rigour > applicability.
notes: CAM only (valerian, melatonin-as-supplement etc.).

title: Identifying complementary and alternative medicine recommendations for insomnia treatment and care: a systematic review and critical assessment of comprehensive clinical practice guidelines.
authors: Zhao FY, Xu P, Kennedy GA et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 17 comprehensive insomnia CPGs to Jan 2023 (7 databases + NCCIH + 6 guideline-developer sites)
keyFindings: 17 CPGs, 14 moderate-to-high quality; RIGHT reporting 42.9-97.1%; 22 CAM modalities; only consensus: valerian, chamomile, kava and aromatherapy not recommended.
conflictsOfInterest: Authors declare no commercial or financial conflicts.
notes: PROSPERO CRD42022369155. Useful cross-guideline table for supplements/CAM; not drugs.

title: Traditional Chinese medicine for insomnia: Recommendation mapping of the global clinical guidelines.
authors: Ye Z, Lai H, Ning J et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 13 insomnia CPGs (international + Chinese databases, NICE, GIN) to 5 Mar 2023
keyFindings: 13 CPGs, 211 recommendations (127 evidence-based, 84 consensus); scope & purpose highest (58.1%), applicability lowest (13.0%); 74.8% (n=95) of evidence-based recommendations rest on low or very low certainty evidence.
conflictsOfInterest: Authors declare no conflict of interest.
notes: TCM focus; 'recommendation mapping' method is a model HCF could reuse for drugs.

title: Prescribing and deprescribing guidance for benzodiazepine and benzodiazepine receptor agonist use in adults with depression, anxiety, and insomnia: an international scoping review.
authors: Brandt J, Bressi J, Lê ML et al.
conditions: insomnia, depression, anxiety (benzodiazepines and Z-drugs: prescribing and deprescribing)
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 113 guidance documents: Asia 11, Europe 34, North America 37, Oceania 7, South America 4, International 20; insomnia-specific 25
keyFindings: 113 documents; by condition: depression 28, anxiety/OCD/PTSD 42, insomnia 25; only 18 specific enough to count as deprescribing documents; concordant that BZD/BZRA are not routine first-line; most common recommended maximum duration under four weeks; inconsistent on drug choice, dosing, as-needed vs regular; tapering approaches 'differed substantially'.
whatWasRead: abstract (full text free, not read in full)
conflictsOfInterest: No funding. Most authors are advisors/directors of the Alliance for Benzodiazepine Best Practices (non-profit); Wright paid as its former medical director.
notes: The most thorough multi-country drug-level comparison found, but limited to one drug class and searched to Oct 2023. Does not cover orexin antagonists, doxepin, melatonin, trazodone. Data-charting table could be a direct seed for HCF rows.

title: Deprescribing benzodiazepine receptor agonists taken for insomnia: a review and key messages from practice guidelines.
authors: Lee JY, Farrell B, Holbrook AM
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: One guideline (Canadian 2018 BZRA deprescribing guideline) summarised
keyFindings: Summarises key messages of the evidence-based BZRA deprescribing guideline (Pottie 2018).
conflictsOfInterest: Not stated in abstract (authors include guideline developers).
notes: Not a comparison; listed so it is not mistaken for one.

title: Quality assessment of clinical practice guidelines for adult obstructive sleep apnea: A systematic review.
authors: Xu X, Peng Q, Meng L et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 44 adult OSA CPGs published Jan 2013-Dec 2023 (42 English, 2 Chinese)
keyFindings: 44 CPGs; clarity of presentation highest (85.10%), rigor of development lowest (56.77%); overall RIGHT reporting 51.30%; 'review and quality assurance' reporting 15.91%; AGREE-RIGHT correlation r = 0.808.
conflictsOfInterest: Authors declare no conflict of interest.
notes: Quality only; does not compare recommendations (e.g., HSAT eligibility, CPAP thresholds, drugs). Paywalled.

title: Guidelines on the surgical management of sleep disorders: A systematic review.
authors: Mandavia R, Mehta N, Veer V
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 22 surgical guidelines from eight countries (to April 2018); 14 adult, 5 child, 3 both
keyFindings: 22 guidelines from eight countries; mean overall AGREE II score 3.5 (range 2 to 5.3, max 7); no UK guideline found.
notes: Surgery only; stale (search 2018).

title: Screening for obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in children and adolescents with obesity: A scoping review of national and international pediatric obesity and pediatric OSA management guidelines.
authors: Ng NBH, Lim CYS, Tan SCHL et al.
journal: Obesity reviews : an official journal of the International Association for the Study of Obesity
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 30 national/international pediatric obesity guidelines + 10 pediatric OSA guidelines
keyFindings: 16 of 30 (53%) pediatric obesity guidelines include OSA screening 'with no consistent recommendations on when and how to screen'.
notes: Scoping review, Singapore. Only pediatric-OSA cross-guideline comparison found; narrow question.

title: Iron Deficiency and Sleep/Wake Behaviors: A Scoping Review of Clinical Practice Guidelines-How to Overcome the Current Conundrum?
authors: McWilliams S, Hill O, Ipsiroglu OS et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 58 iron-deficiency guidelines
keyFindings: Of 58 iron-deficiency guidelines only 9 mention RLS and 3 ADHD; ferritin cutoffs varied.
notes: Shows RLS iron advice is not harmonised outside sleep-society guidelines.

title: The AASM Guidelines for the Treatment of Restless Legs Syndrome (RLS) in the Context of Latin America.
authors: Parejo K, Jimenez-Correa U, DelRosso LM
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: AASM 2024 RLS guideline applied to Latin America
keyFindings: Notes difficult access to gabapentinoids, continued dopamine-agonist use, frequent benzodiazepine use, limited opioid availability, limited iron testing in Latin America.
conflictsOfInterest: Authors are ALADS president and World Sleep Society secretary.
notes: Only RLS cross-region item found; qualitative.

title: Pharmacological management of insomnia with a focus on GABA(A) receptor positive allosteric modulators and orexin receptor antagonists.
authors: Unger C, Kohlmeier KA
conditions: chronic insomnia (GABA-A modulators vs orexin antagonists)
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: Literature review; comments on European vs other approval
keyFindings: States 'Approval for use of orexin receptor antagonists for management of insomnia is more restrictive in European countries than that seen in other regions'.
notes: Regulatory comparison asserted, not tabulated; claim needs checking against EMA/national labels.

title: Global trends in the consumption of benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in 67 countries and regions from 2008 to 2018: a sales data analysis.
authors: Ma TT, Wang Z, Qin X et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 67 countries and regions, 2008-2018, IQVIA MIDAS sales data
keyFindings: BZD use fell -1.88%/yr (95% CI -2.27 to -1.48); Z-drugs rose +3.28%/yr (+2.55 to +4.01); 2008 top ten all European, 63.69-128.24 DDD/1000 inhabitants/day; <1 DDD/TID in Russia, Kuwait, UAE, Saudi Arabia, French West Africa, Philippines; higher use with higher GDP.
notes: Broadest consumption comparison; sales data, not indication-specific; ends 2018 (before orexin antagonists in most markets). Free on OUP.

title: Global trends in antidepressant, atypical antipsychotic, and benzodiazepine use: A cross-sectional analysis of 64 countries.
authors: Alabaku O, Yang A, Tharmarajah S et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 64 countries (33 high, 6 middle, 25 low income), Jul 2014-Dec 2019, IQVIA MIDAS
keyFindings: BZD baseline rates 1.66, 1.46, 0.33 standard units per population (high/middle/low income); 5-year change -13%, +4%, -5%.
notes: Class-level only.

title: Exposure to benzodiazepines (anxiolytics, hypnotics and related drugs) in seven European electronic healthcare databases: a cross-national descriptive study from the PROTECT-EU Project.
authors: Huerta C, Abbing-Karahagopian V, Requena G et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 7 databases in Spain, UK, Netherlands, Germany (Bavaria), Denmark, 2001-2009 (PROTECT-EU), common protocol
keyFindings: Crude prevalence 570-1700 per 10,000 person-years; standardized change Spain +13%, UK +2% and +8%, Dutch -4% and -22%, German -12%, Danish -26%; median 18% of users had ≥10 prescriptions in 2008; hypnotics outweighed anxiolytics in UK and Denmark.
notes: Method model: common protocol across databases. Stale (2009).

title: Use of benzodiazepines and benzodiazepine-related drugs in the Nordic countries between 2000 and 2020.
authors: Højlund M, Gudmundsson LS, Andersen JH et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden, 2000-2020, national registers
keyFindings: 2020 therapeutic intensity from 17 DDD/1000/day (Denmark) to 93 (Iceland); Z-drugs (BZRD) 55-78% of use in 2020; highest prevalence age ≥80.
conflictsOfInterest: Some authors report unrelated industry consultancy/regulator-mandated study funding (Lundbeck Foundation, Otsuka, AbbVie-funded centre).
notes: Good Nordic register data; free.

title: Prevalence, country-specific prescribing patterns and determinants of benzodiazepine use in community-residing older adults in 7 European countries.
authors: Lukačišinová A, Reissigová J, Ortner-Hadžiabdić M et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: Czech Republic, Serbia, Estonia, Bulgaria, Croatia, Turkey, Spain; 2,865 community-dwelling adults 65+, 2019-2020
keyFindings: 14.9% BZD users; Croatia 35.5%, Spain 33.5%, Serbia 31.3%; diazepam 27.9%, alprazolam 23.7%, bromazepam 22.8%, lorazepam 16.7% of users; vs Croatia OR from 0.49 (Spain) to 0.01 (Turkey).
notes: Survey sample, not population data.

title: The prevalence and prescribing patterns of benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in older nursing home residents in different European countries and Israel: retrospective results from the EU SHELTER study.
authors: Lukačišinová A, Fialová D, Peel NM et al.
conditions: benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in nursing homes
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 7 European countries + Israel, 57 nursing homes, 4,156 residents, SHELTER 2009-2014
keyFindings: 27.7% used BZD/Z-drugs; 44.1% Israel to 14.5% Germany; zopiclone 17.8%, lorazepam 17.1%, oxazepam 16.3%; Z-drugs-only strongly linked to France (OR 21.0, 95% CI 9.0-48.9).
notes: Shows drug choice tracks country, not patient need. Stale data (2009-2014).

title: Dispensing of benzodiazepines and benzodiazepine-related drugs in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania: a cross-national drug utilisation study.
authors: Essink SCM, Lasys T, Santa-Ana-Tellez Y et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, 2019-2023, national prescription databases
keyFindings: 2023 prevalence 94.0 (Estonia), 102.0 (Latvia), 117.6 (Lithuania) users/1,000; therapeutic intensity 121, 92, 97 DDD/user.
notes: Recent; open access.

title: International Comparison of Benzodiazepine Prescription for Older Adults in Acute Care Hospitals.
authors: Watanabe K, Austin CA, Umegaki H
conditions: benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in hospitalised older adults
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: One US hospital (UNC) vs one Japanese hospital (Nagoya), 2023-2024
keyFindings: UNC geriatrics BZD 21.9%, ZD 0.7%; UNC other medicine BZD 30.1%, ZD 1.5%; Nagoya geriatrics BZD 7.9%, ZD 3.6%; Nagoya other BZD 7.8%, ZD 5.3%.
notes: Two sites only; letter.

title: Contribution of prolonged-release melatonin and anti-benzodiazepine campaigns to the reduction of benzodiazepine and Z-drugs consumption in nine European countries.
authors: Clay E, Falissard B, Moore N et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: Nine European countries, IMS sales data
keyFindings: 'Campaigns aiming to reduce the use of BZD/Z-drugs failed when they were not associated with the availability and market uptake of PR-melatonin.'
conflictsOfInterest: Not stated in PubMed record; check full text for manufacturer funding (PR-melatonin = Circadin).
notes: Possible industry interest; treat causal claim with caution.

title: Long-term use of benzodiazepines in chronic insomnia: a European perspective.
authors: Soyka M, Wild I, Caulet B et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: France, Germany, Italy, Spain, UK pilot physician survey + literature review
keyFindings: BZDs and Z-drugs most widely used and used beyond recommended ≤4 weeks; country variation in prescription rates (numbers in full text).
conflictsOfInterest: Three authors Idorsia employees (daridorexant maker); others have multiple industry honoraria.
notes: Industry-authored; free full text has country data not extracted here.

title: Policies for Deprescribing: An International Scan of Intended and Unintended Outcomes of Limiting Sedative-Hypnotic Use in Community-Dwelling Older Adults.
authors: Shaw J, Murphy AL, Turner JP et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: International scan of policies (prescription monitoring, delisting, pay-for-performance, rescheduling alprazolam, driving rules, campaigns)
keyFindings: Prescription monitoring: highest discontinuation but inappropriate substitution; insurance delisting: more out-of-pocket cost, minimal impact; pay-for-performance ineffective; alprazolam rescheduling shifted use; driving and education campaigns most promising.
notes: Only policy-level comparison found; countries named in full text (free).

title: Gender differences in adolescent anxiolytic, hypnotic and sedative use across 32 European countries: a multilevel analysis of the influence of country-level gender inequality and economic factors.
authors: Martinez-Mendia X, Bacigalupe A, Moreno-Llamas A
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 32 European countries, ESPAD 2019, 96,954 students aged 15-16
keyFindings: Gender gap wider where gender inequality higher (PR 1.18 low GII vs 1.49 high GII); country context explained 6.7% of variance.
notes: Self-report lifetime use; not prescribing.

title: Where are the Behavioral Sleep Medicine Providers and Where are They Needed? A Geographic Assessment.
authors: Thomas A, Grandner M, Nowakowski S et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: Worldwide provider directories/listservs; 752 providers
keyFindings: 88% of 752 BSM providers worldwide in US (n=659); 4 US states with none; 105 of 167 US cities >150,000 have none.
notes: Data c.2015; directory-based so non-US providers under-counted. Free (PMC).

title: The European Academy for Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Insomnia: An initiative of the European Insomnia Network to promote implementation and dissemination of treatment.
authors: Baglioni C, Altena E, Bjorvatn B et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: Europe (ESRS / European Insomnia Network task force)
keyFindings: Task force statement: across Europe 'hypnotic medication still is the dominant therapeutic modality'; proposes European CBT-I Academy and stepped-care model.
notes: Position paper, not a country-by-country survey of availability.

title: Chronic Insomnia Disorder across Europe: Expert Opinion on Challenges and Opportunities to Improve Care.
authors: Ellis J, Ferini-Strambi L, García-Borreguero D et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: Europe (expert opinion)
keyFindings: Typical European patient: presents to primary care, not offered CBT-I, gets sleep hygiene then drugs, uses GABA-receptor agonists beyond approved duration; tabulates indications/warnings of old and new drugs.
conflictsOfInterest: Most authors report honoraria from Idorsia and other companies.
notes: Describes regional differences qualitatively; no country table of standards in abstract. Free (MDPI).

title: Increasing access to evidence-based insomnia care in the United States: findings from an American Academy of Sleep Medicine stakeholder summit.
authors: Schotland H, Wickwire E, Aaronson RM et al.
journal: Journal of clinical sleep medicine : JCSM : official publication of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: United States only (AASM summit, 50 participants)
keyFindings: Barriers: limited access, low awareness, low perceived value, too few trained clinicians; priority: reimbursement, workforce.
conflictsOfInterest: One author salaried by Nox Health (Somryst owner); another consults for Idorsia, Eisai, Merck, ResMed.
notes: Single country.

title: Disseminating cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) for insomnia at scale: capitalising on the potential of digital CBT to deliver clinical guideline care.
authors: Espie CA, Henry AL
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: International (conceptual)
keyFindings: Argues dCBT can deliver guideline care at scale via stepped-care framework.
conflictsOfInterest: Not stated in PubMed record; first author Espie co-founded Big Health (Sleepio) - verify in full text.
notes: No country comparison of dCBT-I reimbursement; none found anywhere in literature search.

title: The need to prioritize "insomnia disorder" in public health agendas: "a wakeup call" position paper from European and Canadian experts in sleep and mental health.
authors: Palagini L, Arango C, Bassetti CLA et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: Europe, Switzerland, UK, Canada
keyFindings: 'While some countries reimburse evidence-based treatments, others fail to recognize insomnia as a chronic condition'; pathways 'suboptimal across countries'.
conflictsOfInterest: Extensive industry ties (Idorsia, Eisai, Jazz, many others).
notes: Mentions reimbursement differences; check full text (free) for a country table.

title: Melatonin Use in Pediatrics: Evaluating the Discrepancy in Evidence Based on Country and Regulations Regarding Production.
authors: Skrzelowski M, Brookhaus A, Shea LA et al.
journal: The journal of pediatric pharmacology and therapeutics : JPPT : the official journal of PPAG
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: US vs other countries (melatonin regulation and trial location)
keyFindings: Melatonin 'regulated differently around the world with the least amount of regulation placed on OTC supplements in the United States'.
notes: Only melatonin cross-country regulatory paper found; no country table in abstract. Free.

title: Validated UHPLC Methods for Melatonin Quantification Reveal Regulatory Violations in EU Online Dietary Supplements Commerce.
authors: Vanhee C, Degrève C, Boschmans N et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: EU; Belgium limits used as reference; 50 supplements tested
keyFindings: Melatonin in EU is prescription or OTC medicine 'depending on the country' and allowed in supplements with country-specific limits; 12% of legal-supply samples violated rules or had ≥3x Belgian limit.
notes: Analytical chemistry paper; confirms EU patchwork but does not tabulate it.

title: Management of obstructive sleep apnea in Europe.
authors: Fietze I, Penzel T, Alonderis A et al.
conditions: obstructive sleep apnea (diagnosis, CPAP titration, reimbursement, specialist qualification)
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 21 European countries, 38 physicians (2010 questionnaire)
keyFindings: Broadly consistent pathways (referral to sleep physicians, objective diagnosis mainly PSG, CPAP standard; follow-up need 90.5%); CPAP/APAP ratio 2.24:1; titration from home APAP with portable monitoring (38.1%) to in-hospital PSG+APAP (85.7%); differences in reimbursement, titration, qualification.
notes: Baseline for item below. Paywalled.

title: Management of obstructive sleep apnea in Europe - A 10-year follow-up.
authors: Fietze I, Laharnar N, Bargiotas P et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 26 countries, 36 sleep centres (20 ESADA, 6 non-ESADA), survey 2020
keyFindings: Diagnosis by specialized physicians 86% (2010) vs certified sleep specialists and specialized physicians 69% (now); APAP in hospital 73%, at home 62%; HSAT use 76% to 89%; PSG-only diagnosis 24% to 12%; sleep specialist qualification available 52% to 65%; telemedicine diagnostics 8%, treatment 50%, follow-up 73%.
notes: Best existing multi-country OSA pathway comparison. One or two centres per country answering for a whole country; reimbursement detail per country is in full text (free on ScienceDirect per OpenAlex). Not machine-readable.

title: Access and models of obstructive sleep apnea care: a cross-national comparison of Canadian and Australian patient survey data.
authors: Fatima D, Sweetman A, Lovato N et al.
journal: Journal of clinical sleep medicine : JCSM : official publication of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine
conditions: obstructive sleep apnea (wait times, providers, treatments)
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: Canada (589 patients) vs Australia (412 patients) survey
keyFindings: First contact usually primary care in both; sought care within 12 months: 37% Canada vs 51% Australia; diagnostic test within 3 months: 59% vs 76% (urban 58% vs 78%); >80% offered PAP in both; more treatment variety in Australia.
conflictsOfInterest: Funded by CIHR, NHMRC and university grants.
notes: Only patient-side two-country pathway comparison found.

title: Current practice, clinical perspectives and barriers to multi-night testing for obstructive sleep apnea in Europe: a survey across ESADA centers.
authors: Karkala A, Kalkanis A, Başoğlu ÖK et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 43 clinicians, 28 centres, 15 European countries (ESADA)
keyFindings: Over 80% think single-night AHI not robust; 83% agree multi-night testing reduces misclassification; only 7/28 centres use multi-night protocols; barriers: staffing, reimbursement, no guidelines; Western Europe most mature.
conflictsOfInterest: Some authors report ResMed, Boehringer, Fisher & Paykel speaking fees.
notes: Recent (2026).

title: Treatment choice in mild to moderate sleep apnoea in the European Sleep Apnea Database.
authors: Fridriksson B, Hedner J, Zou D et al.
conditions: obstructive sleep apnea (PAP vs oral appliance)
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: ESADA centres across Europe; 10,109 patients with mild-moderate OSA
keyFindings: 6,618 (65.5%) PAP vs 3,491 (34.5%) mandibular advancement devices; MAD use by centre 0% to 76%; MAD accessibility OR 2.3 (1.8-2.9) and reimbursement OR 1.5 (1.4-1.7) predicted MAD recommendation.
conflictsOfInterest: First author one-off fees from ResMed, AstraZeneca, GSK; Grote has institutional and EU grants (full list in paper).
notes: Direct evidence that reimbursement, not guidelines, drives treatment choice. Free.

title: Clinical practice patterns and unmet needs in the use of GLP-1 receptor agonists in sleep medicine: A pan-European survey performed in the European sleep apnoea database network.
authors: Testelmans D, Bonsignore MR, Pataka A et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 24 centres, 14 European countries (ESADA), 2026
keyFindings: 42% of centres say sleep physicians can start GLP-1RA; 92% (symptomatic) and 81% (asymptomatic) still recommend sleep study after starting; 61% use >10% weight loss as reassessment trigger; proactive PAP re-titration 14%; structured pathways 'largely absent'.
notes: Only cross-country practice data on tirzepatide-for-OSA found.

title: Adherence with positive airway pressure therapy for obstructive sleep apnea in developing vs. developed countries: a big data study.
authors: Drager LF, Malhotra A, Yan Y et al.
journal: Journal of clinical sleep medicine : JCSM : official publication of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: Brazil, Mexico, United States; 4,181,490 ResMed AirView patients
keyFindings: 90-day CMS adherence: Brazil 71.7%, Mexico 66.4%, US 74.0%; engagement-app use 8.1%, 2.8%, 26%.
conflictsOfInterest: Funded by ResMed; authors received ResMed fees.
notes: Industry data; applies US CMS definition to all countries.

title: Implementation of European national driving regulations for obstructive sleep apnoea: challenges and recommendations.
authors: McNicholas WT, van der Werf YD, Hartley S et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 25 of 27 EU states + 8 non-EU European states (~770 million people)
keyFindings: All EU members transposed Directive 2014/85/EU, largely unchanged, some stricter (mild OSA, minimum treatment period); only 5 of 8 non-member states had OSA driving rules; implementation problems in most countries.
conflictsOfInterest: Funded partly by Horizon 2020 'Sleep Revolution' (grant 965417); other author grants listed.
notes: Thorough on one narrow topic; country table in free full text — good HCF source.

title: Barriers to the diagnosis and treatment of obstructive sleep apnea in 15 francophone Sub-Saharan African countries: A multicountry survey.
authors: Ouédraogo AR, Adambounou STA, Massongo M et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: 15 francophone sub-Saharan African countries (national experts), Oct-Dec 2025
keyFindings: PSG in 6/15 (40%), polygraphy 13/15 (86.7%); PSG €221-686, polygraphy €69-259; CPAP in 8/15 (53.3%), MAD 5/15 (33.3%); CPAP €381-3,812, MAD €38-305; CPAP insurance (partial) in 3 countries; <2 trained practitioners per million in most.
notes: Rare low-income comparison.

title: Moving toward Equitable Care for Sleep Apnea in the United States: Positive Airway Pressure Adherence Thresholds: An Official American Thoracic Society Policy Statement.
authors: May AM, Patel SR, Yamauchi M et al.
journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: US CMS vs Australia, England, Canada, Japan coverage models
keyFindings: CMS long-term coverage requires PAP ≥4 h/day on 70% of days over 30 consecutive days within first 90 days; Australia, England, Canada: no adherence requirement for coverage; Japan: in-lab PSG plus sleep-practitioner visits every 1-3 months for the whole of therapy.
conflictsOfInterest: COI section not captured in extract; ATS policy statement - check disclosures.
notes: Only payer-rule comparison found; five countries, short prose.

title: New management pathways for follow-up of CPAP-treated sleep apnoea patients including digital medicine and multimodal telemonitoring.
authors: Pépin JL, Baillieul S, Bailly S et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: Europe / international (conceptual)
keyFindings: Reviews telemonitoring-based follow-up; notes need to re-evaluate CPAP reimbursement policies 'in some countries'.
notes: Not a country comparison.

title: Global practice of sleep medicine: Iran.
authors: Behkar A, Amirifard H, Samadi S et al.
journal: Journal of clinical sleep medicine : JCSM : official publication of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: Iran (single country; part of JCSM 'Global practice of sleep medicine' series)
keyFindings: Progress in training and accredited clinics; shortage of specialists and certified clinics; treatment access barriers.
conflictsOfInterest: Authors used ChatGPT for language editing; other COI not captured.
notes: Series format gives one-country snapshots, not comparable fields. Only one series article surfaced in PubMed title search; others may exist under other titles.

title: The Global Initiative for Obstructive Sleep Apnea (GIFOSA): Rationale, Strategic Framework, and Call to Action.
authors: Duong-Quy S, Chirakalwasan N, Desudchit T et al.
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: Global initiative (GIFOSA), Asia-heavy author group
keyFindings: Framework paper: context-sensitive care pathways, task-sharing, tech diagnostics across resource levels.
conflictsOfInterest: COI list truncated in record; check.
notes: Signals that a global OSA pathway effort is starting (2026) but has no comparison data yet.

title: Health at a Glance (2023 and 2025 editions): chronic and long-acting benzodiazepine use in people aged 65 and over
authors: OECD
countriesOrGuidelinesCovered: OECD countries reporting the indicator (search snippet says 18 countries for 2013-2023 trend)
keyFindings: NOT VERIFIED (page returned HTTP 403; figures come only from a web-search summary): 2025 edition reportedly gives average chronic use falling from 33 to 27 per 1,000 people 65+ (2013-2023), range from below 1 (Italy) to 92.8 (Iceland); long-acting use from 64 to almost 42 per 1,000. 2023 edition reportedly 39 to 28.2 (2011-2021), range <1 (Italy, Türkiye) to 87.5 (Iceland).
